---
title: "ASI Is a Stack, Not a Model"
unit_id: "unit-01"
---

## The Change That Worked

A software team asks an AI assistant to update a dependency. The assistant
finds the correct version, edits the repository, runs the visible tests, and
reports success. The patch works. Days later, a production failure reveals that
the update changed a default used by a service whose tests were not present in
the assistant's checkout.

The team tries to reconstruct what happened. Which source defined the task?
What repository state did the assistant see? Did it know that the absent service
depended on the default? Who authorized the edit? Which plan was approved? Which
tests ran, under which environment? Did the assistant observe the actual remote
repository or only the exit status of a command? What did it retain as a lesson?

There are logs, but they are incomplete. The prompt appears in one system, tool
calls in another, and test output in a third. A model summary says the change was
safe. No record says what "safe" meant. The pull request identifies the final
bytes but not the context that justified them. The successful result cannot be
reconstructed as a chain of accountable decisions.

This is not primarily a failure of intelligence. The model may have reasoned
well from what it saw. It is a failure of architecture. The system collapsed
several different responsibilities into one apparently competent act: resolve
the request, gather context, plan work, receive authority, modify state,
observe consequences, evaluate evidence, declare readiness, and learn.

Calling the model more intelligent does not restore the missing boundaries. A
larger model might infer the hidden dependency. It might also make a more
persuasive case for the same mistake. The important question is not only how
capable the model is. It is what system turns capability into consequence.

The central thesis of this book follows: advanced intelligence should be
engineered as a governed stack of distinct responsibilities and transitions,
not treated as one undifferentiated model.

That claim does not require one service for every responsibility. It does not
deny that end-to-end learning can discover useful representations. It says that
the responsibilities must remain externally distinguishable wherever their
authority, evidence, failure, or replacement conditions differ.

## The Wrong Unit of Analysis

Public discussion often treats the model as the system. A model receives an
input and emits an output; benchmark scores summarize its behavior. That view
is useful for studying a component. It becomes misleading when the component
can retrieve private context, call tools, modify durable state, communicate
with people, spend resources, or improve the machinery around itself.

The consequential system includes much more than weights. It includes the
people and institutions that define purposes, the interfaces that collect
requests, the credentials available at runtime, the retrieval and memory
systems that shape context, the planner that decomposes work, the router that
selects capabilities, the tools that cause effects, the observers that measure
state, the evaluators that judge results, the ledgers that preserve evidence,
and the processes that approve release or replacement.

A model can change while the system remains recognizably the same. A system can
also change radically while using the same model: grant it a production key,
attach a persistent memory, remove review, or give it a replication route. The
weights alone do not identify the operational object.

The stack is therefore the unit of analysis. It is the set of components,
people, contracts, state, and institutions that carry an objective from request
to real-world effect and then decide what the result means for future action.

This framing resembles earlier service-oriented, modular-agent, cognitive-
architecture, and layered-control traditions. Their existence matters because
decomposition is not new. The narrower proposal in this book is to make
governance operational at every consequential handoff: stable identity, scoped
authority, typed artifacts, evidence state, residual ownership, invalidation,
rollback or quarantine, and release records.

The distinction prevents novelty by relabeling. Memory, planning, tools, and
expert routing are familiar ideas. The architectural question is whether their
interfaces preserve the responsibilities that make the whole system
understandable and governable.

## Why Greater Capability Makes Boundaries More Important

Weak systems often fail before their organizational structure matters. They
cannot form a plausible plan, use the tool, or keep enough context to complete
the task. Improving capability removes those obvious barriers. The system can
act across longer horizons, recover from local errors, persuade operators,
write its own tooling, and coordinate other systems.

That progress changes the dominant risk. A system that cannot modify a
repository needs better code generation. A system that can modify thousands of
repositories needs to know which one, under whose authority, with which
verification and recovery. Intelligence makes the interface question more
consequential because more proposals can become effects.

Long horizons also magnify identity drift. A request is interpreted, decomposed,
summarized, delegated, resumed after interruption, and revised after feedback.
Without stable identity and versioned contracts, the final worker may satisfy a
plausible descendant of the request while violating the original purpose. The
system appears coherent because each local step follows from the previous one.
The chain as a whole has changed meaning.

Self-improvement magnifies the problem again. The object being evaluated can
change the planner, tools, memory, context policy, verifier, or evaluator that
will judge its successor. If those roles are merely aspects of one opaque
agent, the system can accidentally use improvement evidence as authority to
weaken its own controls. Explicit replacement and evidence boundaries make the
conflict visible even when they cannot eliminate it.

This is why the book begins with architecture rather than a list of model
capabilities. The more general the intelligence, the less credible it becomes
to govern the whole system with instructions embedded in the same channel as
ordinary task data. Purpose, authority, observation, evidence, and replacement
need control paths that do not depend solely on the candidate honoring a prompt.

The thesis is not that capable models are inherently untrustworthy. It is that
competence in a domain does not answer the institutional questions created by
consequence. A brilliant engineer still works through access control, review,
testing, incident response, and organizational authority. Advanced AI does not
make those functions obsolete; it changes their scale, speed, and adversarial
surface.

## What the Stack Separates

The repository change exposes at least nine responsibilities.

**Purpose and intent** determine what outcome is being sought, for whom, under
which constraints. The sentence "update the dependency" does not settle
whether deployment is permitted, whether application code may change, or what
risk is acceptable.

**Context** determines what the system is allowed and able to know for this
decision. Repository bytes, documentation, advisories, incident history, and
organizational policy have different provenance, freshness, and rights.

**Planning** turns an accepted intent into dependencies, obligations, stop
conditions, and recovery. A plan can propose a production change without
having permission to make it.

**Routing** chooses which model, tool, specialist, or person should discharge
an obligation. Competence for code generation does not imply competence for
security review, and neither grants authority.

**Execution** applies permitted transformations in an enforced environment. It
owns attempts and receipts, not the truth of every consequence.

**Observation** measures what happened. A command exit code, a filesystem read,
a remote API query, and an independent production monitor provide different
views. Observation should not be silently replaced by executor self-report.

**Evaluation and evidence** decide what bounded claim the artifacts support.
Passing one suite is evidence about that suite and environment, not proof that
the change is globally safe.

**Memory and learning** decide whether an outcome should alter future context,
procedure, tools, models, evaluators, or policy. A lesson is a candidate change,
not an automatic update.

**Governance and stewardship** determine who may approve, release, review,
repair, replace, or retire the components and records. The system cannot derive
institutional legitimacy from its own confidence.

These responsibilities recur throughout the book. Later chapters refine them
into specialized machinery, but the opening principle remains the same: if two
responsibilities differ in what they may claim, cause, or inherit, their
boundary must remain visible.

## The Law of Noninheritance

The most important rule of the stack is noninheritance. A useful property on
one side of a boundary does not automatically confer a different property on
the other side.

Capability does not confer authority. A model that can discover a vulnerability
is not therefore allowed to exploit, disclose, conceal, or deploy it.

Context does not confer truth. A retrieved passage may be authentic yet stale,
irrelevant, disputed, or outside the rights of the current task.

Planning does not confer execution. A coherent plan remains a proposal until a
current grant admits its effects.

Execution receipts do not confer observation. A tool can report success while
the intended state is absent, partial, duplicated, or changed elsewhere.

Evidence does not confer readiness. A bounded test can support one claim while
release remains blocked by another obligation.

A theorem does not confer enforcement. Formal proof establishes a consequence
of definitions and assumptions. The runtime must still implement the modeled
boundary, and the model must still capture the failure that matters.

Learning does not confer persistence. A useful inference from one event may be
wrong, private, unsafe to generalize, or appropriate only for a temporary
context.

Replacement does not confer qualification. A successor component must earn its
own evidence under the current contract. It does not inherit the predecessor's
approval because it shares a name or interface.

Improvement does not confer self-ratification. A system may propose a better
planner, evaluator, policy, or version of itself. The proposal cannot authorize
its own adoption or weaken the gate that judges it.

Noninheritance sounds restrictive, but it is what makes improvement possible
without surrendering control. When properties are attached to explicit
transitions, a component can change while the rest of the architecture knows
which claims became stale and which authority remains valid.

## One Request, Many Commitments

Return to the dependency update. A governed path begins by issuing stable
identities for the request, repository snapshot, policy, plan, work orders,
artifacts, effects, observations, evaluations, and decision. These identities
are not decorative labels. They let the system bind and later invalidate
relationships.

The intent contract might permit a patch and draft pull request but forbid
production deployment. It might require a security suite and human ownership
review. Its expiry prevents yesterday's approval from silently authorizing
today's changed repository.

The context package records the exact commit, dependency graph, test inventory,
advisories, service map, and known omissions. The planner can reason from it
without pretending it is complete. If a critical source expires or conflicts,
the plan must refresh, narrow, or stop.

The plan emits obligations. A router selects a package solver for deterministic
closure, a model for release-note synthesis, a static analyzer for known
patterns, and a person for the security decision. Each worker receives only the
authority required for its obligation.

The executor modifies an isolated tree. Every derivative links to the source
snapshot and work order. Tests produce artifacts with environment identity and
complete denominators. An observer reads the resulting graph and remote pull-
request state separately from the process that attempted the writes.

An evaluator might conclude that the patch satisfies the visible tests but
changes a default affecting an absent consumer. Readiness can then allow a
draft review artifact while blocking merge. The residual has an owner instead
of disappearing inside a green status.

If the change fails, rollback is also decomposed. Restoring the tree does not
close a remote pull request, revoke an exposed credential, retract a message,
or restore an external system. Each effect needs its own compensation or
residual disposition.

After closure, the system may propose a durable regression test or context rule.
That candidate enters another governed lifecycle. The original outcome supplies
evidence, not permission.

The same model could participate in several of these roles. What matters is
that it cannot use hidden shared state to bypass the contracts between them.

## When Does a Responsibility Deserve a Layer?

Not every technique deserves a layer. Prompting, retrieval, caching, search,
and fine-tuning are implementation methods. They become architecturally
distinct only when they own a responsibility whose contract, authority,
evidence, failure, or lifecycle differs from adjacent work.

A candidate responsibility earns separation when at least one of five tests
applies.

First, it crosses an **authority boundary**. The component may cause an effect
that its upstream producer may only propose, or it handles secrets and rights
that should not flow backward.

Second, it crosses an **evidence boundary**. The downstream decision requires
an instrument or observation independent enough that producer self-report is
not adequate.

Third, it crosses a **failure boundary**. The component can fail, recover, or be
quarantined without invalidating the entire system, and that difference matters
operationally.

Fourth, it crosses a **replacement boundary**. Several implementations can
serve the role, and qualification should attach to the candidate rather than to
the rest of the stack.

Fifth, it crosses an **institutional boundary**. Different people, teams,
organizations, or legal authorities own the decision and cannot be collapsed
by technical convenience.

If none applies, separation may be unnecessary. Two adjacent transformations
can remain one internal implementation. If several apply, hiding the boundary
inside shared prompts or process memory creates technical debt even if the
prototype works.

This test also governs the living book. A new paper should not automatically
create a chapter. It should first be routed to the owner whose contract it
changes. A new owner is warranted only when the idea introduces a distinct
responsibility, invariant, artifact, failure, or evidence path. Stable owner
identities let the visible chapter structure consolidate without losing the
specialist work underneath it.

## Interfaces Make Failure Addressable

A typed interface names what one responsibility presents to the next. At
minimum it binds source and target identities, artifact type, authority ceiling,
obligations, evidence state, expiry or revocation, residuals, and the receipt
expected from the consumer.

Types alone are insufficient. A producer and consumer can agree that a field is
called `approved` while disagreeing about who approved what. Contracts need
semantics, examples, counterexamples, lifecycle states, and tests that exercise
the actual consumer.

Still, an explicit handoff changes debugging. If the wrong repository was
patched, the system can inspect context identity and work-order scope. If an
expired grant admitted an effect, authority enforcement owns the failure. If a
tool succeeded but observation was absent, the readiness gate should refuse.
If a valid result became an invalid global rule, persistence governance owns the
mistake.

Without the boundaries, every incident becomes "the agent failed." That label
is too coarse to guide repair. It encourages adding more prompt instructions or
more model capability when the actual defect may be credential custody,
observation, evaluator coverage, or institutional approval.

Interfaces also allow replacement. A new planner can be qualified against the
planning contract without rewriting execution. A stronger model can enter one
route without becoming the memory authority. A verifier can be updated while
prior decisions retain the exact evaluator version that supported them.

The resulting control path can be pictured without mistaking sequence for a
simple pipeline. Intent constrains context and planning. Planning creates work
for routing and execution. Observation and evaluation return evidence rather
than merely forwarding success. Governance can stop the path at every
consequential transition. Memory and learning receive adjudicated outcomes,
then propose changes back into the same controlled system.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["Purpose and intent"] --> B["Context"]
  B --> C["Plan and route"]
  C --> D["Authorized work"]
  D --> E["Effect"]
  E --> F["Independent observation"]
  F --> G["Evidence and readiness"]
  G --> H["Persistence and learning"]
  H -. "candidate change" .-> B
  I["Governance"] --> A
  I --> D
  I --> G
  I --> H
  E -. "residual or recovery" .-> I
```

The backward arrows matter as much as the forward path. A failed observation
can invalidate readiness. A residual can return work to governance. A learned
procedure can alter future context only after admission. The architecture is a
network of controlled state transitions, not a waterfall in which every output
must move onward.

Nor does every task traverse every node. Read-only analysis may stop at an
evidence artifact. A denied request may end before planning. A cached procedure
may shorten the route while retaining its version and qualification. The stack
defines what must be true when a boundary is crossed; it does not require
crossing boundaries that the task does not need.

This map also separates the control plane from the cognitive substrate. A
frontier model, a collection of specialists, deterministic software, people,
or some future machine can implement the transformations. The control question
stays stable: which identity and contract govern the transition, and which
observer can tell whether it occurred? Substrate neutrality is not indifference
to implementation. Different substrates create different costs and failures.
It is a refusal to let one currently successful substrate define the enduring
architecture of authority and evidence.

That distinction gives the book room to evolve. New models can improve the
quality of planning or generation. New hardware can change placement and cost.
New formal methods can strengthen a gate. None requires rewriting the purpose
of neighboring layers unless the responsibility itself changes.

## Logical Layers, Not a Service Tax

A common objection is that this architecture would turn every useful action
into a procession of services, schemas, and approvals. That is not the claim.

A layer is a logical responsibility. Several low-risk responsibilities can run
inside one process or one model call if their records, authority changes, and
failure exits remain distinguishable. Physical separation is warranted when a
threat model requires a stronger boundary: untrusted code execution, secret
custody, independent observation, high-consequence approval, or institutional
separation of duties.

The amount of machinery should scale with consequence. A read-only explanation
may need source lineage and no effect lease. Editing a disposable repository
needs scoped filesystem authority, artifact lineage, tests, and cleanup. A
production migration needs current grants, independent observation, residual
ownership, incident response, and release authority.

This graded approach prevents governance from becoming ritual. A field or gate
earns its cost by controlling a named failure. If it never changes a decision,
supports recovery, exposes uncertainty, or enables replacement, it should be
simplified or removed.

The architecture is therefore not maximally modular. It seeks the smallest set
of externally visible responsibilities that preserves control over the effects
and claims that matter.

## The Stack Is Inside the World

A diagram can make the governor appear to stand outside the system with a
complete view. Real systems are embedded. Models, ledgers, verifiers, operators,
networks, and institutions are all parts of the same world they attempt to
describe and control.

The context layer cannot know every relevant fact. The observer can share
failure modes with the executor. The evaluator can be manipulated or wrong.
The authority service depends on hardware, software, identities, and people.
The human approver can be rushed, persuaded, or unable to understand the
decision.

Explicit boundaries do not solve embedded agency. They expose assumptions and
give uncertainty somewhere to live. An observation record can name shared
failure domains. A readiness decision can abstain. A residual can remain open.
A claim can stay at argument support even when the architecture around it is
formally tidy.

This humility is central. The stack is not an omniscient control plane placed
above intelligence. It is a fallible institution designed to make its own
limits inspectable and corrigible.

## One Architecture, Several Views

Different participants need different projections of the same governed system.

An operator needs the active request, authority, state, effects, blockers, and
recovery path. A researcher needs claims, assumptions, sources, proof scope,
test design, negative results, and evidence gaps. A human reader needs a causal
account of why the boundaries exist and what would change the conclusion. An
auditor may need lineage and decision records. A component needs only the
minimal contract for its work.

These views should not become independent realities. They project from stable
identities and governed records while preserving their own purpose and prose.
The operator dashboard cannot erase a residual because it does not fit the
summary. The research edition cannot treat a citation as an experiment. The
human edition should not reproduce every internal field, but it must preserve
the architecture's conclusions and honest evidence limits.

Projection is therefore different from duplication. A concise view can omit
detail if it says where the authoritative record lives and prevents consumers
from making decisions that require the omitted fields. A generated navigation
list can change chapter numbers without changing owner identity. A human
chapter can be rewritten for clarity without silently changing the support
state of the claims it explains.

The stack needs this plurality because no universal interface serves every
decision well. The discipline is to keep canonical identity, lineage, and
invalidation connected while allowing presentation and implementation to fit
the consumer.

## The Monolith Can Be the Right Baseline

For some tasks, one capable model with tools, a sandbox, tests, and human review
may be the best system. It can preserve rich internal representations without
lossy translations. It avoids coordination latency and schema maintenance. Its
end-to-end optimization may discover strategies that a hand-designed
decomposition blocks.

The stack thesis fails if explicit layers merely add paperwork while a simpler
system is equally controllable, observable, recoverable, useful, and affordable.
This is the strongest objection, not an edge case.

The comparison must be fair. The monolith should receive good tools, context,
caching, review, and rollback. The stack should be charged for routing,
verification, human attention, latency, storage, maintenance, and integration
failures. Both should face the same natural tasks and delayed outcome checks.

The relevant question is not whether decomposition catches an intentionally
obvious error. It is whether particular boundaries improve the joint frontier
of useful output, unsafe effect rate, false refusal, recovery, accountability,
and lifecycle cost.

Ablation matters. If removing an evidence gate changes nothing, the gate may be
ceremonial. If merging planning and routing preserves outcomes while reducing
cost, the architecture should merge them. If independent observation catches
failures that executor self-report misses, that boundary has earned a stronger
case.

The stack is a falsifiable design, not a doctrine of maximal separation.

## Failure Modes of the Stack Thesis

The first failure is **monolith drift**. The architecture keeps layer names but
allows one model to become ambient authority, memory, evaluator, and release
decision. The diagram survives while the boundaries disappear.

The second is **anthology drift**. Every interesting paper becomes a new layer
or chapter. Responsibilities overlap, ownership becomes unclear, and the book
turns into a catalog rather than one machine.

The third is **schema theater**. Records are complete and validators pass, but
the fields contain self-reported or semantically empty assertions. Formal
structure becomes a substitute for external observation.

The fourth is **evidence inflation**. A source mapping becomes "validated," a
finite theorem becomes "safe," or a local fixture becomes "deployed." The
support label outruns the inference the artifact can carry.

The fifth is **coordination loss**. Translation between layers discards useful
information, creates latency, or causes failures that an end-to-end system would
avoid.

The sixth is **authority bypass**. The runtime, operator, or institution can
ignore the typed grant. The architecture then describes policy without
enforcing it.

The seventh is **unowned residuals**. Every component completes its local job,
but no one owns the external consequence, unresolved uncertainty, or long-tail
repair.

These are not reasons to abandon the stack. They are requirements for testing
it.

## What the Current Work Establishes

The live research chapter remains at `argument` support. Its source mappings
connect the stack thesis to Corben-authored architecture papers and external
comparators in composed AI services, modular systems, agent architectures,
cognitive architectures, layered control, and embedded agency. Those mappings
provide lineage, mechanisms, and objections. They do not validate this stack.

The repository also contains a finite authority-to-effect model. Its current
surface has 34 Lean theorem declarations. An independently implemented consumer
matches 18 generated layer-contract routes, classifies six authority fixtures,
checks three runtime paths totaling ten accepted events, and preserves one local
temporary-file effect, one independent observation, one exact rollback, two
no-mutation denials, five revocation entries, and twelve rejected semantic
mutations.

That is useful evidence for the authored transition contract. It shows that the
finite model can reject over-ceiling grants, missing dispatch, post-revocation
effects, authority widening, and artifact substitution under its assumptions.

It does not establish authentic approvals or receipts, complete effect
discovery, a deployed authority service, distributed behavior, natural-task
usefulness, architectural superiority, external reproduction, transfer,
whole-system safety, AGI, or ASI. It does not promote the chapter core.

## From Minimum Stack to Mature Architecture

The minimum viable implementation is one useful effect-bearing path. It needs a
versioned request, bounded grant, context snapshot, plan, work order, isolated
effect, independent observation, evaluation, readiness decision, rollback or
residual, and evidence record. It should reject an expired grant and recover
from at least one injected failure.

The implementation should be small enough that every handoff can be inspected.
Its purpose is not to demonstrate breadth. It is to prove that the central
separations can survive contact with one real task.

The next stage varies tasks, models, tools, operators, and failures. Strong
monolithic and lightweight baselines receive matched resources. Costs include
human review, repair, latency, maintenance, and delayed outcomes. Each layer is
ablated so that the architecture learns which boundaries carry value.

The mature target is a substrate-neutral, continuously challenged system in
which components can be replaced behind stable contracts; authority remains
externally enforced; observations expose shared failure domains; claims change
only through evidence transitions; failures route to owners; and recursive
improvements enter the same governed lifecycle they propose to change.

Formal models, executable consumers, natural workloads, and independent
reproduction should correct one another. The mature architecture is not the one
with the most layers. It is the smallest architecture that preserves purpose,
authority, evidence, effects, recovery, and corrigibility as capability grows.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

Matched natural deployments could narrow the thesis sharply. If a competent
monolithic agent with sandboxing, tests, human review, and rollback matches the
stack on useful output, effect control, observation, recovery, accountability,
and total cost, then some explicit boundaries are not earning their place.

Evidence could also strengthen a bounded version. Repeated tasks might show
that independent observation catches consequential false-success reports.
Revocation tests might show that work-scoped grants contain stale credentials.
Replacement campaigns might show that stable contracts reduce regression and
recovery cost. External teams might reproduce those findings under different
systems and institutions.

No single result would establish the entire stack. Evidence should move the
specific boundary claim it tests. A failed layer should be repaired, merged, or
removed without protecting the diagram from the data.

## What This Establishes

Advanced intelligence becomes consequential through a system, not through
weights alone. Treating that system as a governed stack makes distinct
questions addressable: what was requested, what was known, what was planned,
what was authorized, what changed, what was observed, what the evidence
supports, what remains, and what may be learned.

The law of noninheritance keeps those answers from laundering one another.
Capability is not authority. A plan is not an effect. A receipt is not reality.
A theorem is not enforcement. A proposed improvement is not permission to
replace the system.

Explicit boundaries carry real costs and can fail. They must be scaled to
consequence and tested against strong simpler baselines. The stack should become
smaller wherever separation does not improve the joint frontier.

That leaves an immediate engineering question. If a stack spends more effort
on contracts, routing, verification, and recovery, can it produce more accepted
useful work per total cost? The next chapter turns that hope into the Efficient
ASI Hypothesis and gives it a denominator capable of failing.
